opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first problem is that we don't really have a good definition of what "human-level intelligence" even means. People throw that phrase around as if it's a single, well-defined threshold, like a finish line we're going to cross. But human intelligence isn't one thing. It's this incredibly rich mix of capacities: perception, common sense, abstraction, analogy-making, social understanding, the ability to learn from very few examples and transfer that knowledge flexibly to new situations. So when someone says "we'll have human-level AI by 2040," my first question is, what exactly are you predicting? How would we know if we got there?

The second problem is historical. If you look back at the history of AI, people have been making these predictions since the very beginning. In the 1950s and '60s, very smart people like Herbert Simon and Marvin Minsky said we'd have machines that could do any work a human can do within twenty years. And that pattern has repeated over and over. The goalpost is always about twenty or thirty years away. I think that tells us something about how we systematically underestimate how hard intelligence really is.

Part of that underestimation comes from what I've called fallacies in how we think about AI. One is the assumption that narrow intelligence is on a continuum with general intelligence: that if a system gets really good at chess or Go or even language tasks, we've taken a step along a smooth path toward general intelligence. But it's not clear that's true. Another is that the things that are easy for us, like recognizing a situation, understanding what's going on in a scene, or knowing basic intuitive physics, turn out to be really hard for machines, and vice versa. We tend to be impressed by machines doing things that are hard for us, and that gives us a distorted sense of progress.

We also tend to use very anthropomorphic language. We say a system "understands" or "reasons" or "learns," and we then attribute to it the kind of understanding a human would have. But often when you probe these systems carefully, you find they're relying on shortcuts, statistical associations that don't generalize the way human understanding does. They can be brittle in ways that are surprising if you assume they understand the way we do.

So I'm not saying it's impossible, and I'm not saying there hasn't been remarkable progress. There has. But I think these specific timeline predictions rest on a lot of assumptions that haven't been examined carefully, and on a pretty shallow picture of what intelligence actually is. I'd rather we spend our effort understanding intelligence better, both in machines and in ourselves, than putting dates on something we can't yet define.

r001.rationale: It says there is no good definition of “human-level intelligence” and asks what the 2040 prediction means or how achievement would be recognized.

r002.rationale: It does not mention subconscious processes or their share of human intelligence.

r003.rationale: It questions assumptions about general intelligence and machine understanding, but does not challenge transferring intelligence from brains to computers without accounting for the processes that ground it.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, there are a few things. The first is that we've heard this before, many times. Herbert Simon said in 1965 that machines would be capable of doing any work a man can do within twenty years. Marvin Minsky said something similar. And every time, the predictions were made by very smart people who were looking at genuinely impressive progress and extrapolating from it. The problem is that the extrapolation keeps failing in the same way, and I think it's because of something I've called the "first-step fallacy" — this idea that if you've made progress on a problem, you're on a continuum that leads to the full solution. Climbing a tree is not the first step toward getting to the moon, even though you're going up.

The second thing is that these predictions almost never define what they mean by "human-level intelligence." It's treated as if it's a single thing, a point on a line, and we're moving along the line toward it. But intelligence isn't one-dimensional. When people say a system has reached human-level performance on some benchmark, that tells you about the benchmark, not about the system's understanding. We've seen over and over that systems that look like they've mastered a task turn out to have learned shortcuts — statistical regularities in the data — and they fall apart when you change the task slightly, in ways that wouldn't trouble a person at all.

And the third issue is that we just don't understand what human intelligence actually consists of. A lot of it is things we don't notice — common sense, the ability to form abstractions and analogies, to understand a situation we've never encountered by relating it to things we have. Those capacities are very hard to measure and very hard to engineer, and the field has a long history of underestimating them precisely because they feel effortless to us. So when someone says "2040," what they're really saying is that these problems, which we don't understand and haven't solved, will be solved on a particular schedule. I don't see what the basis for that confidence is. It could happen sooner, it could take much longer. But stating a date gives an illusion of knowledge that I don't think anyone actually has.

r001.rationale: The response says predictions rarely define what “human-level intelligence” means and criticizes treating it as a single point on a line.

r002.rationale: It says “a lot” of human intelligence consists of things people do not notice, including common sense and forming abstractions and analogies, conveying that much of it operates outside awareness.

r003.rationale: The response discusses gaps in understanding and engineering human intelligence, but does not challenge transferring intelligence from brains to computers or address the processes on which intelligence is grounded.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think one problem is that we don’t have a very clear definition of what we mean by human-level intelligence. Do we mean a system that can perform well on a set of tests? Or do we mean something that can flexibly understand and act in the world, learn new things, and adapt to situations it hasn’t encountered before? Those are very different criteria.

AI has made remarkable progress, but it’s also shown us that doing very well on tasks we thought required intelligence doesn’t necessarily give a system the broader understanding we assumed would come with that. A system can be extraordinarily capable in some respects and surprisingly brittle in others.

So when someone says 2040, I want to know what that date is based on. What’s the argument that the abilities we’re still missing will emerge on that schedule? It’s not that I can prove the prediction wrong. It’s that we don’t understand intelligence, or the obstacles ahead, well enough to justify that kind of precision.

r001.rationale: It says there is no clear definition of human-level intelligence and argues that this makes a precise 2040 prediction unjustified.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention subconscious processes or their share of human intelligence.

r003.rationale: The response questions whether current AI capabilities imply broader understanding, but does not challenge transferring intelligence from brains to computers or address the processes that ground it.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the biggest problem is that we don’t really know what we mean by human-level intelligence, or how we would measure it. Humans have many different kinds of abilities, and AI systems have a very uneven profile: they can outperform us at some things and fail at things that seem elementary to us.

These predictions often assume that the progress we’ve seen will continue along the same trajectory—that if we make systems bigger, give them more data and more computation, we’ll get all the way there. But that’s a hypothesis. We don’t know whether our current approaches are missing something fundamental about understanding, abstraction, or common sense.

So I’m not saying it couldn’t happen by 2040. I’m saying we don’t have a scientific basis for assigning that date with much confidence. A prediction like that sounds much more precise than our understanding actually is.

r001.rationale: It says we do not know what human-level intelligence means or how to measure it, making a 2040 prediction ill-defined.

r002.rationale: It does not mention subconscious processes or their share of human intelligence.

r003.rationale: It questions whether scaling current approaches is sufficient, but does not discuss transferring intelligence from brains to computers or accounting for the processes that ground it.
